alt: A triangle with three appeals at its corners: logos, the appeal to reason (“Does this make sense and is it backed up?”); ethos, the appeal to credibility (“Why should I believe this person?”); and pathos, the appeal to emotion and values (“Does this matter to me?”). Kairos, the right moment, sits in the centre.
caption: Reason, credibility, emotion: three routes to persuasion, strongest at the right moment.

after: ## Ethos: the appeal to credibility and character
alt: Ethos can be built before the argument (a title or reputation), within the text (an account of experience) and through the style (precision and courtesy). Six things build trust: knowledge, fairness, shared values, good will, reliable sources and careful language. Exaggeration and errors damage it.
caption: Ethos is the audience’s trust, built before, within and through the writing.

after: ## Worked example 1: classifying the appeals in a passage
alt: The four sentences of the paramedic passage with their primary appeal: twenty-two years’ experience is ethos; the cardiac-arrest statistic is logos; kneeling beside a father is pathos and also ethos; the cost comparison with an ambulance is logos.
caption: Name the primary appeal, acknowledge a secondary one, and link both to the purpose.

alt: A statistic can serve logos by supporting a claim, pathos by arousing fear, or ethos when quoted from a credible institution. Quoting an expert usually builds ethos through authority, but the expert’s reasoning, if explained, can also be logos.
caption: Ask what job the material does in this text, then name the appeal.

after: ## A public-domain example: Anthony's argument from the Constitution
alt: Three bars of growing width: “we, the white male citizens” and “we, the male citizens” are struck through, and “we, the whole people” spans the full width. Below, the sentence works as logos (an argument from the founding text), pathos (a rising rhythm of justice) and ethos (faithfulness to the Constitution).
caption: One sentence can do all three jobs: the logic is not separate from the rhythm.

after: ## Worked example 2: strengthening a missing appeal
alt: Before and after for the quiet-room paragraph. Before, logos is a claim with no evidence, ethos is absent and pathos is mild. After, a survey statistic and a cost argument add logos, local detail adds credibility, and the mock exam week adds a concrete picture.
caption: Diagnose which appeal is weakest, then add it without losing the single claim.
